newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan July consumer prices up 3.3 pct yr/yr.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan July consumer prices up 3.3 pct yr/yr.

text.p: Taiwan's consumer price index was up 3.3 percent in July compared to July 1996, the Directorate General of Budget, Accounting and Statistics said on Tuesday.
The July wholesale price index was down 0.24 percent compared to a year earlier, the directorate said.
The July CPI rise was just slightly below an average forecast for a 3.40 percent rise compiled from an August 4 Reuters Poll of Taiwan economists.

The directorate attributed the relatively high July CPI growth -- the highest single-month year-on-year growth so far in 1997 -- to torrential rains and floods that hit the island in July, damaging crops and temporarily boosting food prices.
In month-on-month terms, July CPI was down 0.08 percent from June, it said.
The poor weather drove vegetable prices up an annual 34.98 percent in July, though this was only 4.04 percent higher that in June, which also was bedevilled by foul weather.
More broadly, July food prices rose an annual 7.35 percent due mainly to the spiking vegetable prices, the agency said.

In the first seven months, Taiwan's CPI grew 1.65 percent year-on-year, well within the directorate's most recent full year 1997 estimate of 2.01 percent and far below the central bank's official 3.0 percent 1997 target.
The directorate's director, Hsu Jan-yau, said he did not expect the central bank's recent interest rate hikes to fuel inflationary pressure in coming months.
"Interest rates only account for about four percent of production costs, and the central bank's hikes were too small to have an effect," Hsu told reporters.
The central bank on Thursday raised the rediscount rate to 5.25 percent from 5.00 and the accommodations against secured loans rate to 5.625 percent from 5.375.
Likewise, Hsu said the Taiwan dollar's recent depreciation against the U.S. dollar would not hike consumer prices.
"The depreciation is still relatively mild compared to other currencies, especially the mark and the yen," Hsu said.
"The depreciation should raise import prices somewhat, but not enough to make a big difference in inflation," Hsu said.
Import prices were down 2.01 percent in July and 4.94 percent for the whole 1997.

Consumer prices (yr/yr) +3.30 +1.83 (revised)
Wholesale prices (yr/yr) -0.24 -1.64 (revised)
